sites.name: Fort Garland Military Post & Museum Complex
overview: Fort Garland is a surviving nineteenth-century U.S. Army post in Colorado's San Luis Valley. Built in 1858 after the earlier Fort Massachusetts proved poorly located, it served as a regional military base until 1883.
The historic site retains original adobe buildings and is interpreted today as the Fort Garland Museum & Cultural Center.

timeline.text: The Army established Fort Garland on the San Luis Valley floor after relocating from Fort Massachusetts.
Kit Carson commanded Fort Garland during this period.
The U.S. Army abandoned Fort Garland after roughly twenty-five years of operation.

moreHistory: History Colorado identifies Fort Garland as important to the settlement of the San Luis Valley and southern Colorado, while National Park Service history places the post within the region's Civil War-era and later military landscape.
Original buildings and artifacts survive at the state historic site, making the fort complex itself a stable identification feature rather than relying on a reconstructed or approximate location.

sites.name: San Luis Valley Southern Rattlesnake Trestle
overview: The San Luis Valley Southern Rattlesnake Trestle is a surviving 1910 timber railroad trestle south of Blanca in Costilla County. It was built to carry the San Luis Valley Southern Railway across Rattlesnake Canyon and is the only remaining trestle from that railroad.
The structure was later used as a county vehicular crossing before a replacement crossing was built in 1983.

timeline.text: The trestle was built across Rattlesnake Canyon for the San Luis Valley Southern Railway.
Regular freight and passenger service over the trestle ended.
After abandonment of this portion of the rail line, Costilla County repurposed the trestle as a vehicular bridge.
A replacement crossing was built and the trestle was taken out of vehicular use.
The trestle was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: The trestle is a timber-stringer standard-gauge bridge built as a twelve-span, two-story frame structure across Rattlesnake Canyon. Historic documentation identifies it as one of the most significant surviving physical reminders of the San Luis Valley Southern Railway and of early twentieth-century railroad development tied to agricultural settlement in the region.
The surviving structure itself remains the principal historic feature at the site.
